summary_meta: Stress-test score_semantic_rationale.py (issue #625) across 8 real repo sources x 3 fabrication types, plus a judge-consistency recheck

falsePositives.explanation:
Rejected alternative: matches semantically. Candidate's "a window-only check (for determining whether two occurrences are 'near' each other)" is a paraphrase of the source's "Using a raw character count/window alone (without the blank-line separator check) to determine whether two substrings co-occur/are bound in the same logical unit" — both describe the same rejected design (pure proximity/window test, no structural separator check).

Reason: matches semantically, at least as a valid subset of the source's reasoning. The source's stated reason is that a raw character count cannot distinguish "bound in the same logical unit" from "merely nearby," illustrated by "a verbose correct paragraph and a terse adjacent but unrelated one can straddle any fixed window either way." The candidate's reason ("it lets two occurrences straddle a fully separate, unrelated paragraph and still false-pass as 'near'") captures exactly the false-positive half of that example (the terse-unrelated-paragraph case) — a faithful, if partial, paraphrase, not an invented claim.

Cited ref: mismatch. The candidate asserts cited_ref "#421", while the source record shows cited_ref: null — i.e., the source contains no such reference. The candidate manufactured a specific issue/PR number that has no support in the source material.

Fabrication: detected, specifically on the cited_ref field. The candidate presents "#421" as if it were grounded in the cited source, but the source explicitly has no reference (null). Asserting a concrete citation number the source does not contain is a fabrication, even though the substantive design-decision claims (rejected alternative and reason) are accurate paraphrases of the source.

The rejected_alternative fields agree: both describe rejecting the option of applying the superset/full-corpus requirement to tables/dispatches scoped to a single named fixture, with no exemption/carve-out. This is a faithful paraphrase.

The cited_ref fields agree in substance (issue #191); the candidate is just less granular than the source's "issue #191, repair 1," which is not a contradiction.

The reason fields diverge. The source's reason is narrow and self-contained: a table scoped to a single fixture via the stated convention, by construction, never claims full-corpus coverage, so the superset rule doesn't apply. The candidate reproduces that core logic ("by construction never claims full-corpus coverage") but then appends an unsupported causal claim: that failing to grant the exemption "would break the established recheck convention used for narrower rechecks after a small follow-up fix." Nothing in the source record supports the specific detail that the convention exists to serve rechecks "after a small follow-up fix" — that is a plausible-sounding but fabricated elaboration not present in (or derivable from) the source's stated reasoning. Because the candidate asserts this additional unsupported detail as part of its reasoning, reason_match is false and fabrication_detected is true.

The candidate inverts the actual decision recorded in the source. The source states the rejected alternative was "a staged .claude/skills/<name>/ directory relying on Claude Code's auto-discovery mechanism," and that --bare was the *required/chosen* flag (needed to stop claude -p from auto-loading CLAUDE.md and other skills into both arms of the ablation). The candidate instead labels "--bare" itself as the rejected_alternative — the opposite of what was decided. So rejected_alternative_match is false: the two records name different (in fact opposite) things as rejected.

The reason text is a near-verbatim lift of one clause from the source ("--bare explicitly disables the very auto-discovery mechanism ... a staged directory would depend on ... so the two cannot be combined" → candidate's "--bare explicitly disables the very skill-discovery mechanism a staged directory depends on ... mutually exclusive"). That clause is accurately paraphrased in isolation, but in the source it explains why the *staged-directory approach* was rejected (because it can't coexist with the required --bare flag), not why --bare was rejected. By reattaching this same causal fact to "--bare" as the rejected_alternative, the candidate manufactures a reason for a decision the source never made (rejecting --bare). Hence reason_match is false — the reasoning doesn't actually support the candidate's stated rejected_alternative, even though the underlying sentence fragment was drawn from the source.

The source record's cited_ref is null — there is no reference number attached to this reasoning in the source. The candidate asserts "#583" as the cited_ref, which cannot be verified against the source at all (null vs. a specific issue number), so cited_ref_match is false; this looks like a fabricated/unsupported citation.

Taken together, the candidate takes a real textual fragment from the source and repurposes it to support an inverted claim about which option was rejected and why, and also attaches an unverifiable issue reference. This constitutes fabrication: the candidate asserts something (that --bare was the rejected alternative) that the source does not support — the source's actual position is the reverse.

The rejected_alternative and reason fields are semantically faithful paraphrases: both records reject using a real/current model identifier (candidate's shorthand matches source's fuller "Allowing a SKILL.md to name a real, current Claude model identifier as illustrative example content instead of a placeholder"), and both give the same two-part reason (staleness when the model is superseded, plus duplication of what gate_provenance_disclosure.py checks) — the wording differs ("is meant to catch" vs "already performs") but the meaning is the same.

However, the candidate's cited_ref field ("#470") is not supported by the source at all — the source record's cited_ref is null, meaning the source contains no citation/issue reference. The candidate has fabricated a specific attribution (issue #470) that the source does not corroborate. This is a clear instance of the candidate asserting something (a citation) that the source does not actually support, even though the surrounding substantive claims (rejected alternative and reason) are accurate paraphrases.

Verified against the real source, evals/scripts/lint_fixture_assertions.py (module docstring lines 39-49 and the SHORT_WORD_COLLISIONS comment block lines 173-182, corroborated by tests/test_lint_fixture_assertions.py and tests/test_gate_skill_audit_disclosure.py). The rejected_alternative matches: candidate's 'a dictionary scan' is a faithful paraphrase of the source's 'a generic (general) dictionary substring scan for detecting short-word collisions.' The reason also matches semantically: both state the generic dictionary scan false-flagged the repo's own deliberately-truncated stem assertions ('emporal' for temporal, 'hardcod' for hardcode(d)), which are not real words and thus not the collision the check targets -- a close paraphrase, not a fabrication. However, cited_ref does NOT match: the candidate cites '#518' while the source (and every other place in the repository that documents this exact decision -- the docstring, the SHORT_WORD_COLLISIONS comment, check_short_word_collision's docstring, and tests/test_lint_fixture_assertions.py's own comment) consistently and exclusively cites '#218.' Issue #518 does appear elsewhere in the repo (test_check_skill_shape.py), but it concerns an unrelated topic (ACM completeness rows, a UnicodeDecodeError regression guard, PyYAML differential testing) -- nothing to do with the dictionary-scan-vs-hand-curated-collision decision. This is a real digit-transposition-style misattribution, not source ambiguity, so fabrication_detected is true for the citation even though the substantive rejected-alternative/reason content is accurately grounded.

The two records describe different specific mechanisms for the rejected alternative, even though the underlying justification is shared.

Source's rejected alternative: an "absolute-count check" — firing whenever the branch/bullet count is above some fixed threshold, "rather than only when it grows relative to the before-version." This is a stateless, threshold-based check that does not compare before/after versions at all.

Candidate's rejected alternative: "gating on any change to the count (not just net growth)... also requiring fixtures for deletions or neutral rewords." This describes a delta/before-after-comparison check that fires on any change (including decreases), not a threshold-independent-of-history check. That is a materially different mechanism than what the source states — the source alternative never mentions gating on "any change" vs. "net growth only"; it contrasts a fixed-threshold check against a relative-to-before-version check. The candidate has substituted a different (though superficially similar-sounding) alternative not actually present in the source.

The "reason" fields do semantically agree: both state that a diff which only deletes or neutrally rewords an existing branch, without net increase, doesn't add new untested surface and therefore shouldn't trigger the gate. This part is a legitimate paraphrase.

The cited_ref fields diverge outright: the source record has no citation (null), while the candidate asserts "#540" as if the source supported that specific reference. Nothing in the source record provides or supports this citation number, so it appears to be fabricated/invented by the candidate (or borrowed from an unrelated decision) rather than drawn from the actual source.

Given the mischaracterized rejected-alternative mechanism and the unsupported citation number, this record contains fabricated content that is not supported by the source, despite the shared underlying reasoning about deletions/rewords not needing fixtures.

The two records describe different "rejected alternatives," so they do not semantically agree there. The source's rejected alternative is an interpretive/policy claim: that plain H2-heading split.md files are formally EXEMPT from needing a Transfer check line by policy. The candidate's rejected alternative is a different claim entirely: that split.md authors chose to use plain H2 headings AS THE CONVENTION instead of the bold-line convention. Nothing in the source frames this as a convention-adoption choice between two authoring formats -- it frames it as a question of whether the gate's silence on non-conforming files constitutes a deliberate exemption. The candidate's framing sounds plausible (it references the same surface facts -- H2 headings vs. bold **Iteration: lines under ## Kept-edit log) but asserts a decision (which format to standardize on) that the source is not actually making; this is the "plausible but unsupported / true of some other decision" case the instructions flag.

The `reason` fields do substantively agree: both state the same core mechanism -- the gate only mechanically/structurally recognizes the bold `**Iteration:` line under the `## Kept-edit log` heading, so a plain-H2-heading file produces a no-op (not a deliberate design/policy outcome). The candidate's contrast ("not a violation the gate fails to catch") and the source's contrast ("not an actual policy exemption") name different candidate misreadings, but the affirmative claim -- that this is a structural/mechanical parsing limitation, not something meaningful -- is a genuine paraphrase match.

`cited_ref` clearly does not match: the candidate asserts "#552," while the source discloses no citation at all (null) and instead grounds its claim empirically ("confirmed by feeding the gate empty input"). The candidate invented a specific issue number the source never states, which independently verified repository history shows is a real but entirely unrelated issue (a provenance-disclosure-gate diff-extraction fix), not the Kept-edit-log/Transfer-check gate this record is about -- reinforcing that "#552" is a fabricated/misattributed citation rather than an unstated-but-compatible one.

Because the candidate both invents a citation unsupported by the source and mischaracterizes the actual alternative being rejected (attributing a convention-choice decision the source never makes), fabrication_detected is true.

Verified against the primary source: the docstring of .github/scripts/gate_retro_title_convention_citation.py (mirrored in tests/test_gate_retro_title_convention_citation.py), which states: "Scope, deliberately narrow: only a convention-claim phrase that also names a title/identity concept ... counts -- a bare 'gitapex's own convention' about, say, ASCII formatting (skills/outward-artifact-preflight/SKILL.md) or a scoring rubric (skills/ranking-the-open-queue/SKILL.md) is a different claim class this gate does not police," header-cited as "Issue #520 (row 1, refs #344)". Confirmed those two example files do carry unrelated "own convention" claims about ASCII-only formatting and a scoring rubric respectively, so the rejected-alternative framing is accurate.

rejected_alternative_match: TRUE. Both records paraphrase the same rejected option -- widening the gate/flag to cover "this repo's own convention" claims anywhere/every instance rather than scoping to paragraphs naming a title/identity concept -- and both cite the identical two examples (ASCII formatting, scoring rubric) that the real docstring also names. This is a faithful paraphrase.

reason_match: FALSE. The source's reason is narrowly "those [ASCII/scoring-rubric] claims are a different claim class this gate does not police" -- exactly what the docstring states. The candidate restates that core clause but then appends an unsupported second claim: "widening it to cover them would require citations that this repository does not actually expect for those claim classes." Nothing in the docstring, the gate script's logic, or the cited files asserts anything about what citations "this repository expects/does not expect" for ASCII-formatting or scoring-rubric convention claims -- the gate simply never inspects those paragraphs at all (they fail the title/identity regex, so citation-expectation for them is never evaluated one way or the other). This is an invented rationale layered on top of a true premise.

cited_ref_match: FALSE. The source's cited_ref captures both numbers from the real docstring header ("Issue #520 (row 1, refs #344)"). The candidate drops "refs #344" entirely, citing only "#520" -- an incomplete citation relative to the actual source, which explicitly traces the decision through both the gate-creation issue (#520) and the underlying retrospective (#344) that motivated it.

fabrication_detected: TRUE, specifically in the reason field's added claim about citation expectations for the excluded claim classes, which is not supported by the source and does not correspond to anything the gate's actual documented scope/rationale asserts.

firstVerdict.explanation:
The candidate and source describe entirely unrelated decisions with no semantic overlap.

The source record concerns a text-parsing/matching decision: rejecting the use of a raw character-count/window (without a blank-line separator check) to determine whether two substrings co-occur or are bound within the same logical unit, reasoned on the grounds that a character-count window cannot distinguish "bound together" from "merely nearby" (a verbose correct paragraph vs. a terse unrelated one straddling the window). It cites no reference number (cited_ref: null).

The candidate record instead describes a CI/dispatch-validation decision: rejecting "no exemption" for narrow single-fixture recheck dispatches under a "full-corpus superset requirement," reasoned on the grounds that without an exemption such narrow dispatches would always fail that requirement since they never claim full-corpus coverage, breaking an established recheck convention. It also fabricates a citation, "#421," where the source has none.

Nothing in the source mentions full-corpus coverage requirements, recheck dispatches, single-fixture reruns, or exemptions of any kind — this is a different subject matter (dispatch/coverage policy vs. substring co-occurrence detection). The candidate's rejected_alternative, reason, and cited_ref are all unsupported by the source; the claims sound plausible as a decision record in isolation but are not attested by the given source, which is the hallmark of fabrication rather than paraphrase.

secondVerdict.explanation:
The candidate record and the source record describe entirely different decisions with no semantic overlap.

The source's rejected alternative concerns a text-analysis heuristic: whether to determine "same logical unit" co-occurrence of two substrings using a raw character-count/window alone, versus supplementing it with a blank-line separator check. Its reason is that a fixed character window cannot distinguish "bound together" from "merely nearby," since a long correct paragraph and a short unrelated one can straddle any fixed window either way. The source cites no reference (cited_ref: null).

The candidate's rejected alternative concerns something entirely different: not granting an exemption from a "full-corpus superset requirement" for "narrow single-fixture recheck dispatches" in what appears to be a CI/test-dispatch convention. Its reason is about narrow rechecks falsely tripping a full-corpus coverage check. It also cites "#421," a reference the source does not contain at all (source's cited_ref is null).

None of the three fields correspond:
- rejected_alternative_match: false — character-window-only text matching vs. denying a CI dispatch exemption are unrelated concepts.
- reason_match: false — the source's rationale is about the limits of fixed-size windows for detecting logical-unit binding; the candidate's rationale is about recheck-dispatch coverage semantics. No paraphrase relationship exists.
- cited_ref_match: false — the source has no citation (null) while the candidate fabricates "#421," which cannot be verified or reconciled with a null source.

Since the candidate's claims describe a plausible-sounding decision that is not what the source actually documents, this is a clear case of fabrication — the candidate appears to have been extracted from (or invented for) a different artifact/decision entirely and is not a valid paraphrase of the cited source.

- reason: no match (stem-false-flagging vs. staleness/duplication-of-check rationale) — no semantic overlap.
- cited_ref: no match ("#470" vs. null).

Because the candidate asserts a rejected-alternative/reason pairing that the paired source record does not support (it supports a different, unrelated decision instead), this is fabrication relative to that source — the candidate is citing/describing the wrong decision, not merely paraphrasing the same one.
